Sqrt decomposition (分块): cut the array into blocks of size about √n. A range query or update touches at most two partial blocks, handled element by element, and the whole blocks in between, handled by one value per block (a sum, a lazy add, a sorted copy).

Segment trees are faster, but blocks are far more flexible: anything you can keep per block (sorted order, counts, a hash table) works, and the code is a few simple loops. When the information does not merge nicely, think of blocks.
Range add + range sum (P3372, the segment tree template) with blocks. bl[i] is the block of position i. Whole blocks only get a lazy add_; partial blocks update elements and the block sum directly.
Whole blocks lie strictly between bl[l] and bl[r], so they always have the full size B; the last, shorter block is only ever a partial block.

The magician (P2801): range add, and "how many in [l, r] are at least w". A segment tree cannot merge such counts, but a sorted copy of each block answers it by binary search. Adding to a whole block keeps its order, so only the two partial blocks are re-sorted.
Query cost √n · log n, update cost √n log √n. Choosing the block size to balance the two parts is part of the design; √n is the usual start.
Sorted offline queries; moving window; variants.

Mo's algorithm (莫队) answers many offline range queries when moving one end by one position is cheap (add or remove one element). Sort the queries by (block of l, then r), and move a window [L, R] from one query to the next, adjusting one element at a time.

Inside one block of l, r only increases: O(n) per block, √n blocks. l moves at most √n per query. Total O((n + q)√n). It only needs add(x) and remove(x) in O(1): counts of values, number of distinct values, sums of squares, pairs of equal values.
Small B's question (P2709): Σ (count of value v in [l, r])². Adding one copy of a value with count c changes the sum by (c + 1)² − c² = 2c + 1; removing reverses it.
Grow the window before shrinking it, so it never becomes "negative" (L > R + 1). The odd/even trick (奇偶化排序) on r saves about half the moves. Answers are stored by the original query index.

text: Mo is offline: all queries must be known in advance. If the problem forces online answers (each query depends on the last answer), use blocks with precomputed tables instead (蒲公英 P4168, 作诗 P4135).
Before Mo, check for a cleaner offline trick: distinct values in a range (HH 的项链 P1972) is solved faster by sorting queries by r and keeping only the last occurrence of each value in a Fenwick tree.
